challenges.name: operating-redis-memory-eviction-persistence
challenges.title: Operating Redis: memory, eviction & persistence
challenges.description: Three statements on the shared Redis instance of CodeDev after learners were logged out and logins started to fail: what volatile-lru evicts, what allkeys-lru would do to sessions, and what AOF with everysec does and does not protect.

questions.question:
One Redis instance holds sessions, rate-limit counters, the leaderboard and the catalog cache.
$ redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy
maxmemory-policy volatile-lru
$ redis-cli INFO keyspace
db0:keys=2140332,expires=61204,avg_ttl=402113
$ redis-cli --scan --pattern 'catalog:search:*' --count 1000 | head -3 | xargs -n1 redis-cli TTL
(integer) -1
(integer) -1
(integer) -1
$ redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys
evicted_keys:48211

Statement: "Because the policy is volatile-lru, Redis makes room by evicting the least recently used catalog:search keys, so the sessions are safe."
questions.explanation: False. volatile-lru only chooses among keys that have an expiry set. The catalog:search keys have no TTL (TTL returns -1), so they are never candidates; the keys that do have one are the sessions, the rate-limit counters and other short-lived keys, about 61,000 of 2.1 million. Those are what the 48,211 evictions removed, which is why learners were logged out. When no key with a TTL is left to evict, volatile-* behaves like noeviction and writes fail with an OOM error. The misconception is that an LRU policy always evicts "the cache": it evicts what the policy lets it see, and cache keys written without a TTL are invisible to every volatile-* policy.

questions.question:
The team considers switching the same shared instance to allkeys-lru.
Sessions are stored as session:<id> with EX 604800 (7 days), refreshed when the learner makes a request.
INFO memory: used_memory_human:3.98G  maxmemory_human:4.00G

Statement: "With allkeys-lru on this instance, Redis can evict the session of a learner who has been idle for a few hours, long before its 7-day TTL, and that learner is logged out."
questions.explanation: True. allkeys-lru considers every key, with or without a TTL, and picks keys that have not been used recently (Redis samples keys and approximates LRU). An idle learner's session is exactly such a key, and the TTL is only an upper bound on its life, not a guarantee that it lives that long. allkeys-lru is a good policy for a pure cache, where losing a key costs one reload; it is the wrong policy for data whose loss logs users out. The usual fix is to separate them: a cache instance with allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu, and an instance for sessions and the leaderboard with noeviction and a memory alert well below maxmemory. The misconception is that a TTL protects a key from eviction.

questions.question:
redis.conf of the instance that holds the leaderboard:
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec
replica-read-only yes
# one replica, asynchronous replication; Sentinel promotes the replica if the primary fails

Statement: "With appendonly yes and appendfsync everysec, a crash of the primary or a failover loses no write that Redis has acknowledged, so lb:global can be the only copy of the scores."
questions.explanation: False. everysec writes the AOF to disk about once a second, so a crash of the machine can lose roughly the last second of acknowledged writes (appendfsync always narrows that window at a large cost in throughput). Replication is asynchronous: if Sentinel promotes the replica, writes that the old primary acknowledged but had not yet sent are lost, whatever the AOF settings of the old primary. Persistence makes a restart much less painful; it does not turn Redis into the source of truth. The scores belong in learner_score in PostgreSQL, and the leaderboard should be rebuildable from it (lesson 3.3). The misconception is to read "durable" in AOF as "no acknowledged write is ever lost".
